title: Why Lean is faster than Rust — kim@lean
excerpt: Notes on Lean, tactics, and making the theorem prover do more work.
content_html:
kim@lean:~$ cat posts/2026·07·24.md

2026·07·24 [performance] [lean]

I can't possibly be serious, can I, claiming that Lean is faster than Rust?

Let me show you something:

# silesia.tar: the 212 MB standard corpus. Each tool compresses at level 6
# and prints the resulting size in bytes; `time` reports wall-clock.
$ time deflate-rust silesia.tar   # miniz_oxide (pure Rust, no 'unsafe')
68112144
real    0m5.79s

$ time deflate-lean silesia.tar   # lean-zip
68054183
real    0m4.87s

What's going on here? This is the lean-zip implementation of DEFLATE compressing the standard silesia compression benchmarking corpus, faster and better than miniz_oxide, the standard pure-Rust implementation.

How is that even remotely possible? The secret is this:

/-- Unified DEFLATE roundtrip: inflating what we deflate returns the input exactly. -/ theorem inflate_deflateRaw (data : ByteArray) (level : UInt8) (maxOutputSize : Nat) (hsize : data.size ≤ maxOutputSize) : inflate (deflateRaw data level) maxOutputSize = .ok data := Zip.Native.Deflate.inflate_deflateRaw data level maxOutputSize hsize

The Lean library isn't just tested and validated, it's proved correct. This allows us to let AIs loose optimizing the code, requiring that they update the proof whenever the implementation materially changes. This gives us the confidence to allow them to work autonomously in a way that would be unthinkable in other languages.

What comes out of this process is astonishing.

These graphs show the "Pareto frontier", describing the compression ratio vs throughput tradeoff for the lean-zip and miniz_oxide implementations. Like all DEFLATE implementations, both libraries have a tunable knob (the "level") that gives better compression in exchange for lower throughput. The way these graphs are set up, further left is better compression, further up is better throughput. The green line shows what you get as you sweep through the levels using miniz_oxide, compressing the silesia corpus. The animated red line shows what you get for lean-zip, over the course of the autonomous optimization process (using a combination of Claude and Codex agents).

(Note these graphs are measuring the geometric mean of the compression ratios across the constituent files in silesia.tar, so it's a slightly different measurement than our first measurement.)

We can't match miniz_oxide's L1 for raw speed: it's 30% faster than our fastest setting, in exchange for compressing 16% worse. Its L2 we simply beat, at very slightly better compression and 20% higher throughput. Through its L3 and L4 we're level, within a percent or two. From L5 on we pull ahead: 8% at L5, 24% at L6 — the typical default for zip algorithms, and where this post's headline numbers come from — and 90% at its L9.

I still can't quite believe that!

You might say, of course "well, no one has tried running these agents on miniz_oxide, trying to optimize it in the same way". And this is certainly fair: I'm sure we could improve the performance! But would we trust it? Are the AIs introducing subtle bugs that aren't picked up by the current test suites? We'd have to carefully audit and review everything it suggests. But on the Lean side we just shrug and say "inflate (deflateRaw data level) = .ok data still holds, so I guess it's fine".

For completeness, here's the Pareto frontier graph showing a number of other DEFLATE libraries:

lean-zip is certainly not the best here: libdeflate unsurprisingly blows it out of the water (unsurprisingly because this is a very carefully tuned implementation using architecture-specific SIMD, that we can't touch in Lean). zlib-ng and zlib-rs are faster than us across most of the range their curves cover, though not at the deep end: their L9 lands at exactly the compression ratio lean-zip reaches at L7, and we reach it at about the same speed as zlib-rs, a few percent ahead of zlib-ng. zlib-ng is optimized C; zlib-rs is a memory-safe Rust implementation heavily based on zlib-ng, with some carefully contained unsafe internally.

We're competitive with or simply better than the other libraries. We completely dominate the OCaml, JavaScript, and zlib C reference implementations, and lose at lower levels but win at high levels against Go, pure Rust (miniz_oxide), and Zig.

There are also some caveats that are worth thinking about:

  • The Lean implementation has higher memory consumption than miniz_oxide.

  • There are some trust gaps because we use Lean's @[extern] annotation to provide a few low-level functions (e.g. word-sized reads from a ByteArray) that are currently missing from the Lean runtime. We're pushing Lean's readiness as a general purpose programming language, so these will probably be added to the runtime soon.

  • Proving that our implementation round-trips, produces a valid DEFLATE stream, and accepts any valid stream, is a good start, but doesn't address other interesting questions, e.g. absence of side channels or verified performance guarantees.

  • Our decompression implementation is still slower: miniz_oxide decompresses about 1.45x faster.

I'm not really claiming that "Lean is faster than Rust". It's still much easier to sit down and produce a performant implementation in Rust than it is in Lean! This experiment merely shows that:

  • It is possible, with lots of tuning, to get basic algorithms written in Lean competitive with implementations in "fast" languages.

  • That effort is happily and surprisingly delegatable to AIs, when you can write theorems characterising the algorithm, allowing aggressive optimization without human review.

Still, it's food for thought, that we can get this close at all!

content_html_zh:
kim@lean:~$ 猫帖子/2026·07·24.md

2026·07·24【业绩】【精益】

我不可能是认真的，对吧，声称精益比 Rust 更快？

让我给你看一些东西：

# silesia.tar: the 212 MB standard corpus. Each tool compresses at level 6
# and prints the resulting size in bytes; `time` reports wall-clock.
$ time deflate-rust silesia.tar   # miniz_oxide (pure Rust, no 'unsafe')
68112144
real    0m5.79s

$ time deflate-lean silesia.tar   # lean-zip
68054183
real    0m4.87s

这是怎么回事？ 这是 DEFLATE 的精益 zip 实现，压缩标准西里西亚压缩基准语料库，比标准纯 Rust 实现 miniz_oxy 更快更好。

这怎么可能呢？ 秘密是这样的：

/-- Unified DEFLATE roundtrip: inflating what we deflate returns the input exactly. -/ theorem inflate_deflateRaw (data : ByteArray) (level : UInt8) (maxOutputSize : Nat) (hsize : data.size ≤ maxOutputSize) : inflate (deflateRaw data level) maxOutputSize = .ok data := Zip.Native.Deflate.inflate_deflateRaw data level maxOutputSize hsize

精益库不仅经过了测试和验证，而且还被证明是正确的。 这使得我们可以让人工智能放松对代码的优化，要求它们在实现发生重大变化时更新证明。 这让我们有信心让它们以其他语言无法想象的方式自主工作。

这个过程的结果是令人惊讶的。

这些图显示了“帕累托前沿”，描述了lean-zip 和 miniz_oxy 实现的压缩比与吞吐量的权衡。 与所有 DEFLATE 实现一样，这两个库都有一个可调旋钮（“级别”），可以提供更好的压缩以换取较低的吞吐量。 这些图表的设置方式，越靠左是更好的压缩，再靠上是更好的吞吐量。 绿线显示了使用 miniz_oxy 扫描各个级别并压缩西里西亚语料库时所得到的结果。 动画红线显示了在自主优化过程中（使用 Claude 和 Codex 代理的组合）您从lean-zip 获得的结果。

（请注意，这些图测量的是 silesia.tar 中各组成文件的压缩比的几何平均值，因此它与我们的第一次测量略有不同。）

我们无法在原始速度方面与 miniz_oxy 的 L1 相匹配：它比我们最快的设置快 30%，但压缩率却低了 16%。 我们以稍微好一点的压缩率和高出 20% 的吞吐量击败了 L2。 通过 L3 和 L4，我们处于同一水平，相差一两个百分点。 从 L5 开始，我们领先：L5 为 8%，L6 为 24%（zip 算法的典型默认值，也是本文标题数字的来源），L9 为 90%。

我还是不太相信！

当然，您可能会说“好吧，没有人尝试过在 miniz_oxy 上运行这些代理，并尝试以相同的方式对其进行优化”。 这当然是公平的：我确信我们可以提高性能！ 但我们会相信它吗？ 人工智能是否引入了当前测试套件未发现的微妙错误？ 我们必须仔细审核和审查它建议的一切。 但在精益方面，我们只是耸耸肩并说“inflate（deflateRaw 数据级别）= .ok 数据仍然有效，所以我想这很好”。

为了完整起见，下面的帕累托前沿图显示了许多其他 DEFLATE 库：

在这里，lean-zip 当然不是最好的：libdeflate 毫不奇怪地把它从水中吹了出来（毫不奇怪，因为这是一个使用特定于架构的 SIMD 的非常仔细调整的实现，我们在 Lean 中无法触及）。 zlib-ng 和 zlib-rs 在其曲线覆盖的大部分范围内都比我们快，但不是在最深处：它们的 L9 恰好达到了lean-zip 在 L7 时达到的压缩比，而我们达到它的速度与 zlib-rs 大致相同，比 zlib-ng 领先几个百分点。 zlib-ng 是优化的 C； zlib-rs 是一个内存安全的 Rust 实现，很大程度上基于 zlib-ng，但内部有一些不安全的地方。

我们与其他图书馆具有竞争力，或者只是比其他图书馆更好。 我们完全主导了 OCaml、JavaScript 和 zlib C 参考实现，在较低水平上输了，但在高水平上战胜了 Go、纯 Rust (miniz_oxy) 和 Zig。

还有一些值得思考的注意事项：

  • Lean 实现的内存消耗比 miniz_oxy 更高。
  • 存在一些信任差距，因为我们使用 Lean 的 @[extern] 注释来提供 Lean 运行时当前缺少的一些低级函数（例如，从 ByteArray 读取字大小）。 我们正在推动 Lean 作为通用编程语言的准备，因此这些可能很快就会添加到运行时中。
  • 证明我们的实现往返、生成有效的 DEFLATE 流并接受任何有效流，是一个好的开始，但没有解决其他有趣的问题，例如缺乏侧通道或经过验证的性能保证。
  • 我们的解压实现仍然较慢：miniz_oxy 解压速度大约快 1.45 倍。

我并不是真的声称“精益比 Rust 更快”。 在 Rust 中坐下来生成一个高性能的实现仍然比在 Lean 中容易得多！ 这个实验仅仅表明：

  • 通过大量调整，用精益编写的基本算法可以与“快速”语言的实现相媲美。
  • 当你可以编写表征算法的定理时，这项工作令人高兴且令人惊讶地委托给人工智能，从而无需人工审查即可进行积极的优化。

尽管如此，我们仍然可以如此接近，这仍然值得深思！
